title: Chapter Three
collection: The Life of St Andrew the Fool

sections.heading: Chapter Three — mocked in the street, and hidden in plain sight

pairs.en: *He prays for the men who make sport of him.* *He tells secrets and things to come.* *In a brothel the women try to move him to lust, and fail.* *He excels in fasting, and in being caught up in prayer.*
**16.** In the morning, when he had said goodbye to me, he went out to his day's work in the spirit, wearing a small cloak.

When he reached the bread-sellers, a gang of loutish young men saw him raving and took hold of him and dragged him into a tavern with them. They sat down with the wine they had bought and began drinking, striking him about the neck; and because they took everything he said for a madman's talk, they would not let him go — while giving him no share at all of the food they were greedily working through.

The righteous man, seeing they had no intention of sharing anything with him, thought over what he should do about them. When one of them set down on the table a cup full of the best wine, he snatched it and drank it off, smashed the cup on the man's head, and bolted for the door. They ran after him, caught him, dragged him back inside, hitting him as they went, and sat down to drink again — giving the righteous man nothing, mocking him, and going on landing blows on his neck.

When the fools had amused themselves with him to their hearts' content, and evening had come on, they wanted to leave the tavern and abandon him there. The blessed man said to them: *Fools, fools!* *What am I to do, when the night watch is going to meet me and I shall get a whipping?*
He said it about **them**. They did not understand. They left him and went off. But the righteous man knew already what was going to happen to them.

**17.** They talked it over and went off to the houses of shameless women, and there they fouled the beauty of their souls until the second watch of the night. The blessed man had gone out and thrown himself down in a corner, like one of the poor.

Afterwards they came out and were walking home, and the watch met them, seized them and tied them up; and coming to the very place where the blessed man was lying, they stripped them and flogged them hard.

Seeing them suffer like that, the blessed man was deeply grieved and overcome with tears, and begged God on their behalf that they might not be shut up in prison. Between their relatives' pleading and the blessed man's prayer they were let go, and went home.
One of them said: *Confound Satan, brothers — the thing that madman of ours said was going to happen to him has happened to us!*
Another said: *Don't you know that when a demon means to do somebody harm, it knows it in advance?* *Perhaps his demon did this to us for what we did to him.*
Another said: *No.* *My guess is that God has paid us back because we beat him without mercy.*

And another said: *Oh yes — you idiot!* *Does God care about that fool?* *He has been handed over to a demon, and we knocked him about for sport; there is nothing remarkable in it.* *If he were a holy man you might convince me that God had paid us back for the wrong we did him.* *But he is out of his wits, so it is no concern of God's.*

**18.** While they were saying this, and the other things young men say, the blessed man was up early and running his course again, keeping himself among the crowds and the noise, never sitting down all day, and passing it without food.

When evening came he walked the porticoes of the city looking out for a place where the dogs made their beds; and finding one, he would drive a dog off and lie down there as though on a couch — naked, with nothing at all, not so much as a rush-mat or a scrap of rug, only the little sheepskin cloak already mentioned, which he wore.

And getting up in the morning he would say to himself: *There you are, Andrew, you miserable madman — you have finished your sleep like a dog among the dogs.* *Come on, let us get back to work, for death is near.* *Let nobody fool you that anyone will be able to help you in that hour: every man eats the fruit of his own labours when his body leaves him.* *So keep running, and keep working, however these men in the world despise you — so that we may win praise and glory from the King of heaven.*
**19.** Saying such things the blessed man pressed on, in the way the Apostle Paul speaks of, straining forward to what lies ahead and forgetting what lies behind.

But the people watching him said: *He has been demon-possessed since he was a boy.* Others said: *This is no place for him among decent people* — and they piled blows on his neck, and spat on him, and found him disgusting.

He bore it all: hungry, thirsty, shivering with cold, burning in the heat. And he took up this prayer in the hidden chamber of his soul, so that the murmur of his lips carried some way off. Just as a pot boiling hard throws off thicker steam, so the vapour of the Holy Spirit went out from within him — so that people watching closely said: *His heart is being tormented by the evil spirit, and that is what gives off the steam.*
It was nothing of the kind. It was unceasing prayer, pleasing to God, that produced it. So the unskilled reasoned about this exactly as men once explained the speaking of tongues as drunkenness.

**20.** One day he was going past the brothels, playing the fool as usual, when one of the women there caught hold of the cheap little sheepskin he had wrapped round himself and dragged him inside. And he — hard as adamant, and a true mocker of Satan — went with her.

Once he was in the house the rest of the women crowded round him and asked him mockingly how he had come to be in such a state. The righteous man only smiled and answered nothing. But they struck him, and pushed him towards the act, handling him, kissing him all over, trying to provoke a chaste man into shamelessness, saying: *Get on with it, fool, and satisfy your soul's desire.*
And it was a marvel, brothers, and an awesome thing, what happened to him then. With all that they did to him they were not able to move him or stir him even slightly towards that rank passion.
So they changed their tune and began saying: *This man is a corpse.* *He is a senseless block of wood.* *He is a stone that will not move.*

But one of them said: *I am amazed you can say such things.* *He is a fool and a demoniac, hungry, thirsty, shivering with cold, with nowhere to lay his head — does he want this?* *Leave him to his madness.*

**21.** And the righteous man saw the demon of fornication standing there in the middle of the women. He looked like an Ethiopian, thick-lipped, with no hair on his head but dung mixed with ashes; his eyes were like a fox's, and a wretched rag hung on his shoulder. A threefold stench came off him — putrid, foul, and like frothing spittle — so that the blessed man was sickened by the bitter reek of it, spitting again and again and stopping his nose with a fold of his garment.

The demon of debauchery, seeing him so disgusted, came out with this: *Men keep me in their hearts like sweet honey, and this mocker of the world loathes me and spits at me!* *So it was not for the good that you made yourself a fool after all — it was to get out of serving as a slave.*

The blessed man perceived him with his own senses. The women heard the voice but saw nobody. And the blessed man laughed at how ugly and how foul he was — so that one of the women said: *Look, he is sharing a joke with his own demon.*
**22.** Then one of them said: *That cloak of his is a good one.* *Let us take it and sell it — that will give us something to drink today.*

They got up at once, stripped him, stood him there naked, and sold the tunic for one miliarision, which they divided among themselves, two lepta each. The first said: *Let us not send him away with nothing — let us at least give him a worn-out rush-mat.* So they brought a rush-mat, split it down the middle and wrapped it round him, and threw him out of the house.

He came into the street wearing it and ran along playing the fool. People who saw him said: *That's a fine little rug you have on your shoulder, madman!* And he would say: *Yes, fools — I am wearing a fine garment, for the Master has made me a patrician.*

Some Christ-loving people used to give him small coins of their own accord, without his ever asking; he never asked, but Christ looked after him. Whatever anyone gave him he took, and over a whole day he would gather twenty lepta, or thirty, or more.

Then he would look out for some out-of-the-way place where the poor gathered, and go there holding the coins in his hand as though he were only playing with them, so that what he was doing would not become known. He would sit down among the poor and toy with the coppers; and whenever one of the beggars managed to snatch some, he would give him a cuff — at which the other poor would come rushing in with sticks to defend one of their own; and using that as his chance to escape, he would scatter every coin as he ran, and each of them would grab something and keep it.

**23.** One day the holy man was going through the Antiphoros, and happened into one of the wine-shops where they were drinking wine flavoured with myrrh. A man came in for a drink, and the holy man fixed his eyes on him and kept staring. The man saw him staring, glared back and said: *What are you looking at, fool?* *Get out.*
The holy man said: *There is a stingy demon sitting on your right shoulder like a little monkey, and he has you on a halter like a bear, you poor wretch.* *Give me a copper.*
The man flew into a rage and said: *I haven't got one.*

The holy man said: *Yes — admit it to your own soul.* *You brought seven folles out of the house.* *One you spent on vegetables, another on lupin-beans, and the five you are carrying in your shirt, and the demons are pushing you to spend them on drink.*

When he had said it, the man was astounded that it was all true and told the whole thing to the others sitting there drinking. The tavern-keeper heard him and said: *Well, I see the rest of you are madder than he is.* *It is not the man speaking, it is the demon that goes about with him.* *So why be astonished?* *Does the demon not know who fornicates, who steals, who is stingy, who has how much hidden away and what he brought out of his own house?* *Since Satan follows a man about, obviously he watches everything he does, his coming in and his going out; and if he is friendly with him, he reports everything to you, other people's business included.*
Saying this, the tavern-keeper convinced them that this was how it was.

**24.** One day the blessed man was going through the bread-market and fell in with three fair-haired young men, handsome in soul as well as body — for they had taken up a good way of life, with an elder guiding them in everything pleasing to God.
When they met the holy man, the first of these dignified youths saw the truth about him and said to the others: *Believe me, my dears, I suspect that fool is a servant of God.*
Another said: *Please — let us sit down with him somewhere.*
The first said: *If you like, I will see to it at once.* And he said to him: *Brother, if you love me, come and sit with us;* *I love you, and my friends here want you very much.*

Seeing this, he smiled and said to him by name: *You are Epiphanios, my friend* — and with the word he embraced him, with his far-seeing eye signalling in advance what was going to become of him: that he was to be bishop of the Queen of Cities.
The two of them went hand in hand to the other two boys, and Epiphanios told them how the man had called him by his name; and hearing it they longed for him and believed in him all the more.

So they went into one of the wine-shops and bought bread and wine and fish and laid out a feast. And the holy man, seeing their faith, rejoiced with great joy, and was murmuring a prayer to God under his breath, commending them for coming to him; and then he shared what had been set out, giving to the young men with his own hands.

**25.** It is true, beloved, and it can be relied on, that he ate half a small dry loaf in a whole day — and even then he took only a little of it and left the greater part on the table. If anyone gave him wine he did not refuse to drink it; but he never drank of his own accord, only when it was given him.

Often for a whole week, or for two or three days, he tasted nothing at all — for Satan hardened most people so that they no longer offered him anything, and since he asked for nothing, he received nothing.

He often burned with thirst, and having no way of getting a drink, would find mud where rainwater had collected on the highway; and kneeling down he would breathe over it three times in the sign of the cross, and drink it. People passing by who saw this were outraged; some of them would beat him, and others would say to him threateningly: *It is not right, fool, to drink filth like that.*
He never answered any of them a word, but simply withdrew.
That, beloved, was the blessed man's diet, and the way of life he kept hidden.

**26.** As I said before, he was sitting eating in the wine-shop with those honourable young men — and it happened that I myself, the least of men, was passing and heard his voice. I turned off the road, stood in the doorway and secretly watched what he was doing.
When the young men had said goodbye to him and gone their way, it happened too that the tavern-keeper, who was a Christian, went out of the shop on some errand, and he was left alone inside.

And the holy man looked this way and that, and seeing nobody there, stretched out his hands on high and made supplication for those three young men — and, as I call God to witness, who destroys those who speak lies, **he was lifted off the ground into the air and hung there**.
So awesome and so beyond nature did it appear to me, dissolute as I am, that trembling took hold of me as I watched, and my mind went out of me.
Then at once he came back to himself, went outside, and carried on his usual behaviour among the crowd. And this is what I now make known to your love.
